name: Cloudflare Workers
summary: Cloudflare Workers runs your backend code on servers at the edge, close to users, for fast APIs and small full-stack apps.

free_plan_covers.note: Free plan allows 100,000 requests a day (about 3M/month), but only 10ms of CPU time per request, which limits heavier logic.

first_paid_usd_month.note: Workers Paid plan is $5/month and includes 10M requests and 30M CPU-milliseconds, then usage-based overage after that.

portability.note: Workers run on a V8 isolate, not Node.js, and apps typically depend on Workers-only KV, R2, D1, or Durable Objects APIs.

runtime_model.note: Code runs on V8 isolates at Cloudflare's edge locations worldwide, not in one region or on a traditional server.

persistent_disk.note: There is no filesystem; use Workers KV, R2, or D1 for any state that needs to persist.

long_lived_connections.note: Workers natively support the WebSocket API; pair with Durable Objects to coordinate multiple clients like a chat room.

background_workers.note: Workers only run in response to a request or a Cron Trigger; there is no always-on background process type.

scheduled_jobs.note: Native Cron Triggers run a Worker on a schedule with no extra service needed.

free_plan_commercial_use.note: No restriction on commercial use is stated for the Free plan, though it has no SLA and only community support.

framework_support.note: Next.js runs via a beta OpenNext/vinext adapter with limited image optimization; static Vite apps deploy directly; SvelteKit's official adapter-cloudflare supports all core features. Express runs with the nodejs_compat flag, and FastAPI is supported on Python Workers. Go only runs compiled to WebAssembly. Spring Boot, Django, Rails, Laravel and ASP.NET Core need Cloudflare Containers, which a Worker starts and which need the paid plan.

custom_domain_free.note: Custom domains work on the Workers Free plan too, as long as the domain itself is added to Cloudflare, even on Cloudflare's free zone plan.

free_plan_sleeps.note: Workers run at Cloudflare's edge and start fresh on each incoming request instead of an always-on process, so there is no inactivity pause or wake-up wait.

bandwidth_included.value: Free and Paid ($5/month) plans: no charge for data transfer to visitors on either plan; you are billed by request count and CPU time instead.
bandwidth_included.note: Cloudflare does not meter bandwidth for Workers at all, so the real limits to watch are the 100,000 free requests a day and 10ms of CPU time per request.

setup.step: Run npm create cloudflare@latest and sign in with a Cloudflare account.
Write your Worker code in src/index.ts and add any bindings (KV, R2, D1) to wrangler.jsonc.
Run wrangler deploy to publish to a workers.dev subdomain or a custom domain.
Optionally connect a GitHub repo in the Cloudflare dashboard for automatic deploys on every push.

builder_notes: Each request gets only 10ms of CPU time on the free plan (30 seconds max on paid); heavy computation, image processing, or large loops will hit the limit fast.
There is no filesystem; use Workers KV, R2, or D1 for any state, and Durable Objects to coordinate multiple WebSocket clients.
Next.js support runs through a beta adapter, not a native runtime; check the compatibility notes before relying on less common Next.js features.
